description:
How long the ground under a block stays too wet to drive on after the water comes off, for one soil. THE HOURS ARE THE WHOLE RECORD: a compaction warning is a clock started by the last irrigation and read against a number, and that number is a property of the SOIL and of nothing else. Sand is back under a tractor before the shift ends; a silty clay is not, and the same twenty-four hours applied to both either keeps machinery off ground that was ready yesterday or sends it onto ground that will hold the wheel ruts for a decade.

IT IS A RECORD RATHER THAN A CONSTANT IN CODE for the reason Pest Action Threshold is: the number is LOCAL. A county soil survey, an extension bulletin and a grower who has watched their own rows for twenty years will give three answers, and the third is usually the right one for that farm. A threshold nobody can edit is one an operator quietly stops believing, and the first thing they stop believing is the colour on a map.

WHICH BLOCK GETS WHICH PROFILE is `Field.soil_profile`. An irrigation zone resolves through the block it waters (`Irrigation Zone.field`), because the soil belongs to the ground and a zone is a way of watering some of it. A zone naming no block, or a block naming no profile, falls back to the shipped default of 24/48 hours and the overlay SAYS SO in `thresholds_source` rather than presenting a guess as a measurement.

THE SEEDED ROWS ARE A STARTING BOOK, NOT YOUR FARM'S. They are drainage-class shapes off the USDA textural classes — what is worth keeping from them is that the spread between a sand and a clay is nearly an order of magnitude, not the particular hour figures. Replace one with your own and nothing overwrites it.

fields.description: The soil, in whatever vocabulary the farm keeps it in. The seeded rows use the USDA textural classes — Sand, Loam, Silt Loam, Clay Loam — because those are what a county soil survey names and what an operator can look their own ground up under. IT IS THE DOCNAME: a profile is referred to by what the soil is called, on a Field form and in an overlay answer, and a hash there would make every reference unreadable.
fields.label: Soil Type

fields.description: How fast this soil sheds water, which is the mechanism behind both hour figures. Recorded beside them rather than instead of them: the class is what somebody recognises from a soil survey, and the hours are what the map actually reads.
fields.label: Drainage Class
fields.options:
Rapid
Well Drained
Moderately Well Drained
Somewhat Poorly Drained
Poorly Drained

fields.description: Untick to retire a profile without deleting it. A block still naming a disabled profile falls back to the shipped default and the overlay names the profile it skipped — a colour that silently changed because somebody retired a row is worse than no colour.
fields.label: Enabled

fields.description: Under this many hours since the water came off, the ground is RED — wet, and a pass over it compacts. Machinery decisions are what this number is for; it is not a statement about whether a worker may walk in, which is the restricted-entry interval and a different register entirely.
fields.label: Red Under (Hours)

fields.description: Between the red figure and this one the ground is YELLOW — drying, and a loaded sprayer is a worse idea than an empty quad. Past it the block is green. MUST BE GREATER THAN THE RED FIGURE and the controller refuses otherwise: a yellow under a red leaves an EMPTY caution band, so every block reads green the moment the red hours pass and the warning that exists to be read is never drawn.
fields.label: Yellow Under (Hours)

fields.description: Where the number came from — 'NRCS Web Soil Survey, Wasco County', 'our own 2024 wheel-rut trial', 'shipped default'. The question asked the first time somebody disagrees with a colour on the map, and the one a seeded figure has to be able to answer honestly.
fields.label: Source

name: Soil Compaction Profile
